metadata.title: Claude, When Not.
metadata.topic: CLAUDE · WHEN NOT TO USE AI
metadata.thesis: Knowing when NOT to use it IS the AI skill.
metadata.bookend_exempt_reason: show-tell bookends are drawn Manim scenes (hesitant writer, term cards, drawn composer, spoken outro) rather than Remotion interface scenes — single-renderer pipeline, same as the other general-audience redos.

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Here is the naive version of this film: let AI do everything for you. And here is the real one: learn when not to use it. That gap is the whole film.
beats.screen: Writer types 'let AI do everything for me', strikes it, writes 'learn when NOT to use it'.

qc.sparse_reason: show-tell single-hero-object composition; waives Gate V underfill and clustered only

beats.narration_text: Four terms, in plain words. A scaffold is a support that helps you climb — you still do the climbing. A crutch is a prop that does the work instead of you. A hallucination is when an AI invents a fact and says it confidently. And disclosure just means saying plainly where the AI helped.
beats.screen: Four term cards: scaffold / crutch / hallucination / disclosure.

beats.narration_text: Here is the thesis, and it is short. The real AI skill is not using AI more. It is knowing when not to use it. Everything else in this film hangs off that one line.
beats.screen: A ladder; a figure climbs; a terracotta check lands at the top.

qc.sparse_reason: show-tell single-hero-object composition; waives Gate V underfill and clustered only

beats.narration_text: So: when to use it. Use Claude for leverage. Quiz yourself on your own material. Get feedback on a draft you wrote. Ask it to explain things that confuse you. Generate practice problems. Plan and schedule. In every one of these, you are in the driver's seat. That is a scaffold.
beats.screen: Scaffold frame draws around the ladder; five rungs light up, one per spoken use; 'scaffold' label.

qc.sparse_reason: show-tell single-hero-object composition; waives Gate V underfill and clustered only

beats.narration_text: And when not to. Do not use it for work you would hand in without saying the AI helped — skipping disclosure is the line. Not for the first draft of anything you are supposed to learn by drafting. Not for facts you will not check. And not for anything you would hide. That last one is the test.
beats.screen: The figure leans on a crutch; a page slips; 'crutch' label; an ink cross lands on the page.

qc.sparse_reason: show-tell single-hero-object composition; waives Gate V underfill and clustered only

beats.narration_text: Here is the one question that collapses all of it. Would you hide this use from your boss, your client, or your readers? If yes — do not do it. Not because you will get caught. Because the hiding means the use is taking something that was supposed to be yours: the skill, the learning, the accountability.
beats.screen: Figure holds a page openly; a second page slides behind its back; a terracotta ring spotlights the hidden page.

qc.sparse_reason: show-tell single-hero-object composition; waives Gate V underfill and clustered only

beats.narration_text: Take drafting. If you are supposed to learn to write, and Claude writes the first draft, you skipped the class — because the drafting was the thinking. Reading a finished draft teaches you almost nothing. Writing it is what teaches you the thing.
beats.screen: A page; draft lines draw in one by one; a crutch arrives and a strike crosses the lines.

qc.sparse_reason: show-tell single-hero-object composition; waives Gate V underfill and clustered only

beats.narration_text: Or take facts. Claude can invent a citation, a date, a quote, and deliver it with total confidence. Researchers call that hallucination. So the rule is simple: if you will not check a fact, do not ask Claude for it. Your name on the output means you checked.
beats.screen: A page of ghost lines; a magnifier sweeps over it; a terracotta check lands with 'check it'.

qc.sparse_reason: show-tell single-hero-object composition; waives Gate V underfill and clustered only

beats.narration_text: Commit before the answer. Which of these is a do-not-use? A: quiz me on a chapter. B: write my report. C: explain a confusing concept. D: give feedback on my draft. One of these skips the learning that was supposed to be yours. Pick it now.
beats.screen: Four option cards in a row: A quiz / B write / C explain / D feedback.

beats.narration_text: It is B. Writing your report skips the drafting, and the drafting was the skill. A, C, and D are all scaffold uses — quizzing, explaining, feedback. You stay in the driver's seat, and Claude stays a tool.
beats.screen: Card B slides away; terracotta checks land on A, C, D; the ladder stands under them.

qc.sparse_reason: show-tell single-hero-object composition; waives Gate V underfill and clustered only

beats.narration_text: So draw the line here. Use AI for leverage, to climb higher than you could alone. Do not use it in place of the thing you are supposed to learn. Scaffold, not crutch. That is the whole card.
beats.screen: A vertical line draws down the frame: ladder and scaffold on the left, crutch on the right; a terracotta check on the left.

qc.sparse_reason: show-tell single-hero-object composition; waives Gate V underfill and clustered only

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: list five things I use you for each week. Run each through the hide-it test — would I hide this use from my boss? Mark each one scaffold or crutch. Then run your own checks: does its verdict match your gut, and would you tape its one-sentence summary to your laptop?
beats.screen: A drawn Claude.ai composer; the prompt types in; two check lines appear: your gut, the laptop test.
